Definition: Affordability of mobile broadband data, measured as the cost of a basic mobile data plan (1-2GB) as a percentage of GNI per capita. The UN Broadband Commission target is below 2% of monthly GNI per capita. Affordability is the single largest barrier to internet adoption in Africa.

revision_notes: Original score of 0/Unknown with no source was not supported by evidence available on a check. Statista reports Senegal's average retail price for 1GB of mobile data at USD 1.63 in 2023 (range USD 0.47-1.63 across 28 plans), against World Bank GNI per capita (Atlas method) of USD 1,630 in 2023 (USD 135.83/month). This gives an entry-level 1GB data cost of approximately 1.2% of monthly GNI per capita, within the 'Affordable (1-2%)' band. No official ITU/A4AI country-level price-basket-as-%-of-GNI figure for Senegal specifically was located in this check; the score rests on a derived calculation rather than a single stated ITU percentage, so medium confidence only. Recommend confirming against ITU's 2024/2025 ICT Price Basket country data when available.
revised_comments: A basic 1GB mobile data plan in Senegal costs around USD 1.63 on average (Statista, 2023, based on 28 plans, with a low of USD 0.47), equivalent to approximately 1.2% of monthly GNI per capita (World Bank GNI per capita, Atlas method, USD 1,630 in 2023). This places Senegal's mobile data affordability within the 'Affordable' band, below the average of around 4% of GNI per capita for a comparable data-only mobile-broadband basket across Africa (ITU, 2024), reflecting a competitive prepaid mobile market with multiple operators (Orange, Free, Expresso).

Definition: Percentage of mobile connections using smartphones (as opposed to feature phones or basic phones). Smartphones are the minimum device requirement for accessing most digital public infrastructure services, apps, and mobile internet.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Original score of 0/Unknown with no source was not supported: GSMA data was readily available. GSMA's Mobile Gender Gap Report 2025 gives internet-enabled phone ownership in Senegal (2024) at 78% of men and 62% of women, a population-weighted average of approximately 70%, which sits within the '60-79%' band. GSMA separately profiles Senegal in its November 2025 'Accelerating Smartphone Adoption in Africa' report as one of eight focus markets, and its December 2025 newsroom release notes the high cost of smartphones as a continuing barrier to closing Senegal's 54% mobile-internet usage gap, consistent with adoption below the near-universal 80%+ band. Medium confidence because the 70% figure is derived from GSMA's gender-disaggregated funnel data (internet-enabled phone ownership as a proxy for smartphone ownership) rather than a single stated country-level smartphone-penetration percentage.
revised_comments: GSMA Intelligence data (Mobile Gender Gap Report 2025) show that around 78% of men and 62% of women in Senegal own an internet-enabled (smartphone-capable) phone, giving a population-weighted adoption rate of roughly 70%, within the 60-79% range. Affordability of handsets remains the principal constraint on further growth: GSMA's November 2025 'Accelerating Smartphone Adoption in Africa' report includes Senegal as a focus market, and its December 2025 country study on Senegal's digital transformation identifies the cost of smartphones as a key driver of the country's remaining 54% mobile-internet usage gap despite near-universal 4G population coverage (97%).

Definition: Affordability of electricity for residential and small business consumers, measured as cost of electricity relative to income levels. High electricity costs are a direct barrier to ICT adoption and data center viability.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Original 0/Unknown with no source was not supported: Senegal's electricity regulator (CRSE) publishes SENELEC's residential tariff schedule and GlobalPetrolPrices reports a December 2025 average residential price of XOF 109.39/kWh (USD 0.19/kWh). Applying the World Bank/ESMAP 'subsistence consumption' benchmark of 30 kWh/month against the first-tier residential tariff (approximately XOF 82/kWh, USD 0.135/kWh) gives a monthly cost of approximately USD 4.05, or about 2.9% of monthly GNI per capita (USD 140, World Bank 2024); using the average blended tariff instead gives approximately USD 5.70, or 4.1% of monthly GNI. Both estimates fall within the 'Moderate (3-5%)' band. Medium confidence as no single primary source states this ratio directly for Senegal — it is calculated here from tariff and GNI data.
revised_comments: Residential electricity in Senegal is billed by SENELEC on a tiered tariff regulated by the CRSE, with the lowest domestic tier (Domestique Petite Puissance) priced at around XOF 82/kWh (approximately USD 0.135) for the first 150 kWh, rising to XOF 159/kWh in higher tiers; the average residential price across all tiers was XOF 109.39/kWh (USD 0.19) in December 2025. Set against a subsistence consumption benchmark of 30 kWh a month and Senegal's GNI per capita of USD 1,680 (2024), this represents around 3-4% of monthly income, placing electricity in the 'Moderate' affordability band, a persistent concern given SENELEC's reliance on imported fuel and government transfers to cover its costs, and one the regulator has flagged for gradual tariff reduction from 2028.

This points to a moderate level of grid reliability, with outages occurring roughly monthly rather than weekly, though a substantial share of firms are still affected and report resulting revenue losses.

Definition: The gap between men and women in mobile internet usage or internet access. Based on the GSMA Mobile Gender Gap data or ITU gender-disaggregated ICT statistics. A smaller gap indicates more equitable access to digital opportunities.

revision_notes: Original 0/Unknown with no source was not supported: GSMA's Mobile Gender Gap Report 2025 gives Senegal-specific 2024 mobile internet adoption rates of 78% for men and 66% for women, a relative gender gap of approximately 15% (calculated as (78-66)/78), narrower than the Sub-Saharan Africa regional average gap of 29%; the report also names Senegal (alongside Pakistan) as a country where women adopted mobile internet at a notably faster rate than men in 2024. Medium-high confidence: derived directly from GSMA's own published country-level percentages rather than a single explicitly stated gap percentage, but based on primary named-country GSMA survey data.
revised_comments: GSMA survey data for Senegal show that 78% of men and 66% of women were using mobile internet in 2024, a relative gender gap of approximately 15 percentage points, narrower than the 29% average gap across Sub-Saharan Africa. Senegal is highlighted by GSMA as one of the few countries where women's mobile internet adoption grew notably faster than men's in 2024, continuing a gradual narrowing of the digital gender divide, although women remain less likely than men to own smartphones outright (62% versus 78%) and to use mobile internet daily (73% versus 81%).
